note: Holdings-relevant market news, researched daily by the intel agent (multi-theme sweep: precious metals, HK tech, SGX/Singapore, rare earths, macro) with sources. The "actionable" line relates each item to this specific portfolio. Not financial advice.

items.headline: Silver crashes to 8-month lows (~$56/oz), down ~7% on the week and ~20% on the month as the Iran war spikes oil and revives rate fears
items.summary: Silver traded near $55.5-56.5/oz on Friday 17 July, its lowest in eight months, capping a ~7% weekly loss and a ~20% monthly slide. Counter-intuitively, the selloff came DURING a geopolitical war: the escalating US-Iran conflict pushed oil up ~13% in five days, reviving inflation worries and expectations the Fed holds or hikes, while a firm dollar and a growth scare hit the industrial-heavy metal. The safe-haven bid never showed.
items.actionable: This is the #1 hit to the levered-silver stack — the metal is trading as a rate/industrial asset, not a haven, so the oil-inflation impulse is the direct threat. Keep leverage sized so the break to 8-month lows can't force liquidation; the big cash pile is the buffer, and a deep-value re-entry only makes sense once the oil spike and hike-tail fade.

items.headline: Gold posts its biggest weekly loss in six, sliding below $4,000 (~$3,970-4,050) as the Iran war fans inflation and hawkish-rate fears
items.summary: Spot gold fell to roughly $3,970-4,053/oz into 17 July — its worst week in six and ~26% below the earlier-2026 peak above $5,500 — as the war-driven oil spike revived inflation and hold-or-hike expectations. The structural floor is intact: the PBoC added 14.93 tonnes in June (a 20th straight month, the largest since 2023) and 89% of central banks expect to keep accumulating. Goldman cut its year-end target to $4,900, JPMorgan its Q4 view to $4,500.
items.actionable: Gold below $4,000 pressures the GDX/miner sleeve, but the central-bank bid is a genuine structural floor — treat ~$3,900-4,000 as the line that matters for the miners. Don't expect gold to rescue silver; both are hostage to the oil-inflation impulse and the 28-29 July FOMC.

items.headline: Oil holds near a one-month high (Brent ~$84, WTI ~$79) as US-Iran war enters a sixth night and a naval blockade throttles Hormuz
items.summary: Crude held elevated as the June truce collapsed and US strikes on Iran continued for a sixth night. Strait of Hormuz throughput dropped to ~7 vessels (from 13 the prior day) after a US naval blockade, and Iran readied the Houthis to threaten the Red Sea route. The oil-driven inflation impulse is the key transmission channel pressuring the Fed and precious metals — up ~13% in five days.
items.actionable: The war premium is a double-edged sword: it lifts any energy exposure but is precisely what's crushing the metals book by reviving the hike tail. Do NOT add to levered silver on the geopolitical spike — the June round showed those safe-haven bids evaporate. Watch for a ceasefire headline as the fast reversal risk.

items.headline: June US CPI falls 0.4% m/m — the largest drop in 6+ years; headline eases to +3.5% y/y, core cools to +2.6%
items.summary: June CPI declined 0.4% m/m (led by a 5.7% drop in energy), cutting annual headline inflation to 3.5% and core to +2.6% y/y (0.0% m/m) — the biggest monthly drop since 2020 and a cleanly disinflationary print. The feared hot core did not materialize. But Chair Warsh cautioned against declaring 'mission accomplished,' and the subsequent oil spike from the Iran war has clouded the disinflation story.
items.actionable: The soft print was the good news the metals book needed — the September-hike tail that crushed silver in June did not get re-armed by the data. But the war's oil spike is doing the Fed's hawkish work anyway, which is why metals fell despite the disinflation. Net: a genuine positive undercut by geopolitics.

items.headline: Fed seen holding 28-29 July but split; hikes (~37%) are the live tail, not cuts — Warsh stays hawkish, data-dependent
items.summary: Markets price ~63% odds of no change at the 28-29 July FOMC vs ~37% for a 25bp HIKE — hikes, not cuts, are the risk. The benchmark has held at 3.50-3.75% all year (last held 17 June). June projections showed the committee split roughly in half between holding and hiking before year-end. Warsh has scrapped forward guidance for pure data-dependence, and the oil spike complicates the soft-CPI read.
items.actionable: A hold-or-hike Fed (no cuts in sight) is the persistent headwind for the rate-sensitive metals and REIT sleeves. Keep the cash pile earning ~3.6-3.75% as dry powder; any TLT/long-duration add should wait for a growth-scare or a genuine dovish shift, not this backdrop.

items.headline: Semiconductor rout deepens: SOX -11% on the month, SMH -9% in four weeks on AI-capex-spending fears; leadership rotates to energy/financials/industrials
items.summary: The semiconductor complex is the market's biggest loser this window — SOX down ~11% on the month and SMH ~9% over four weeks, roughly 20% off the late-June peak — on fears that hyperscaler AI-capex spending has peaked (Micron -8%, Intel -4%). The S&P fell to 7,457.69 (-1.15% on 17 July) as money rotated out of chips into energy, financials and industrials; breadth actually broadened (~68.6% of the S&P above its 200-DMA).
items.actionable: The AI-capex-doubt unwind is a caution for the semiconductor-localization sleeve (SMH, SMIC) and validates Burry's chip shorts — don't catch the falling knife. The silver lining for the book: the rotation is INTO the cyclical/defensive sectors, not a broad breakdown, so ex-tech breadth stays healthy.

items.headline: China Q2 GDP misses at +4.3%, weakest since Q4 2022 — first miss since Covid; exports +27% but property investment -18%
items.summary: China's Q2 GDP slowed to +4.3% y/y, down from 5.0% in Q1 and below the 4.5% consensus and Beijing's target — the first miss since the pandemic. Exports surged 27% (semiconductors, computer parts) but soft domestic demand and the Iran oil shock weighed; property investment fell 18% and fixed-asset investment -5.7%. H1 GDP was 4.7%, raising the odds of a policy response.
items.actionable: A soft China macro is a headwind for the HK-tech sleeve's earnings backdrop, but a big enough miss raises the odds of forceful PBOC/fiscal stimulus — the key upside optionality. Hold the quality names (Tencent) with buyback support; the GDP miss argues for patience over adding aggressively.

items.headline: Hong Kong tech rebounds on AI catalysts: Alibaba ~+11%, HSTECH +300pts; southbound funds pile into Tencent, Meituan, Alibaba
items.summary: The Hang Seng Tech Index rebounded 300+ points off its late-June trough, with Alibaba surging ~11%. Southbound funds bought a net HK$497M (6 July), concentrated in Tencent (+HK$2.32B), Meituan and Alibaba. The rally rotated from AI hardware into internet/application names, fueled by Tencent's Hunyuan Hy3, Meituan's open-sourced LongCat-2.0 and Kuaishou's Kling AI raise (up to $3B).
items.actionable: A tailwind for the HK-tech sleeve (Tencent, SMIC, Xiaomi) as the domestic-AI-application bid and southbound buying return. Size for volatility — these swing 7-12% a session — and note the rotation is now toward internet/apps over hardware, so Tencent's franchise + buyback is the cleaner hold.

items.headline: Singapore STI hits a fresh record above 5,500 (~5,553) on a 10th straight up-session; DBS/OCBC lead
items.summary: The Straits Times Index rose ~1.5% to about 5,553, a fresh all-time high and its 10th consecutive up-session, led by financials and tech/industrial services (DBS +2.1%, OCBC +2.2%, HongkongLand +2.0%). STI earnings growth is seen accelerating to 8.8% in 2026F, with bank earnings turning to +5.4% y/y growth in FY26F. Banks and REITs dominate the Q2 SGX earnings calendar now beginning.
items.actionable: The SGX sleeve (DBS, Singtel, REITs, developers) is riding a record index on a 10-session run — but with banks extended into results at ~2.2x book, favor adding S-REITs (which benefit from a lower SORA) over paying up for banks. DBS reports ~6 August.

items.headline: Lynas deepens ex-China magnet push (JS Link 3,000tpa plant); Malaysia scrutinizes its Pentagon supply deal
items.summary: Lynas — the largest rare-earths processor outside China and first heavy-rare-earth producer ex-China — signed a long-term deal with South Korea's JS Link on 7 July to build a 3,000tpa NdFeB magnet factory in Kuantan, extending downstream. On 16-17 July a Malaysian parliamentary committee reviewed Lynas's role in the US defense supply chain (tied to a $96M March DoD agreement). China's 22 June export-control listing of MP Materials/USA Rare Earth still weighs on the sector.
items.actionable: The Western supply-chain build-out keeps advancing (Lynas magnet capacity + DoD backing), reinforcing the ex-China scarcity thesis — watch LYC.AX/MP/REMX pullbacks as cash-funded scale-in candidates. But note the Malaysian political scrutiny as a Lynas-specific overhang and China's blacklist as the sector's two-way risk.

items.headline: Bitcoin and Ethereum jump on the soft CPI: BTC ~$65k (+4.4%), ETH ~$1,890 (+6.6%); CLARITY Act hearing in focus
items.summary: Bitcoin opened around $64,975 on 15 July (+4.4% d/d) and Ethereum ~$1,890 (+6.6%, with ETH +6% on 14 July) as the softer June CPI lifted risk assets; BTC eased back toward $63k as the Iran risk-off dominated later in the week. Traders are watching the US CLARITY Act market-structure hearing for institutional-flow clarity. BTC remains well off early-2026 highs.
items.actionable: Crypto's pop on the soft CPI and resilience through the war is a mild risk-appetite positive for the book, but keep sizing small — a Fed pivot or CLARITY passage is the needed durable catalyst. Useful as a sentiment gauge more than a core position.

items.headline: Japan advances bill to reclassify crypto as financial instruments — flat 20% tax, TSE spot ETFs by 2027
items.summary: Japan's Upper House committee approved legislation to treat Bitcoin and other crypto as financial instruments under the FIEA, lowering the crypto tax to a flat 20% and paving the way for spot crypto ETFs on the Tokyo Stock Exchange as early as 2027. It is a structural, institutional-access positive for the asset class alongside the US CLARITY Act push.
items.actionable: A medium-term structural tailwind for crypto convexity (widening regulated access), but not a near-term price driver — it strengthens the 12m case for keeping a small crypto sleeve rather than a reason to add today into a fearful, war-driven tape.

items.headline: Xiaomi June EV deliveries +36% to 34,738, a third straight month above 30k; shares rally on the YU7 ramp
items.summary: Xiaomi topped 30,000 EV deliveries for a third straight month (34,738 in June, +36.4% y/y), with YU7 SUV volumes up 64% m/m. Xiaomi and BYD shares rose on the June figures. H1 deliveries exceeded 180,000 against the 550,000 full-year-2026 target, keeping the EV ramp on the growth track that supports the broader Xiaomi story.
items.actionable: A fundamental positive for the Xiaomi holding — the EV ramp is executing and diversifies the story beyond handsets/IoT. Consistent with holding 1810.HK through the tech-sector volatility; the ~HK$20bn buyback (a fresh 3.9M-share tranche on 15 July) adds a corporate bid underneath.

items.headline: Uranium holds firm near $85/lb (rangebound $84-87, +19% y/y) on AI-datacenter nuclear demand
items.summary: Spot uranium sat around $85.45/lb on 16 July, rangebound between $84 and $87 through Q2 and still up ~19% y/y. Support comes from AI-datacenter nuclear demand (Meta, Amazon and Microsoft capacity deals) and geopolitical power-market volatility, offset by muted utility spot buying. The term market's price stickiness underpins the uranium-equity thesis.
items.actionable: A steady uranium price supports the URA/UUUU sleeve's cash-flow floor while the rare-earth optionality plays out — a lower-beta way to hold the critical-minerals/AI-power theme than the volatile rare-earth developers. Watchlist adds on risk-off pullbacks funded from cash.
